planting.note: Direct sow on the soil surface after the last frost once the ground has warmed, since seed needs light to germinate; egoma is grown to full seed maturity rather than harvested young, so plan for a long warm season and let the short autumn days trigger flowering and seed set.

directions: Egoma, called deulkkae in Korean and egoma in Japanese, is the oilseed variety of Perilla frutescens, distinct from the leafy shiso and kkaennip types grown as var. crispa and var. japonica. Its plain, non-wrinkled green leaves and stronger, more resinous perilla-ketone aroma make it less refined as a fresh table herb, but it is prized for its plump seeds, which are toasted and ground into the nutty seasoning deulkkae-garu or cold-pressed into deulgireum (perilla oil), a staple finishing oil in Korean cooking. Like other perilla, flowering is triggered by shortening daylength in late summer, so full-season growth in a sunny bed is needed to bring the seed heads to maturity before frost. Cut whole seed stalks once the lower seed pods begin to dry and rattle, then finish drying upside down in a paper bag to catch the shattering seed.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops — Perilla frutescens
Korea Rural Development Administration (RDA) — Deulkkae (Perilla) Cultivation Guide
Kitazawa Seed Company — Perilla Growing Notes

planting.note: Surface-sow after the last frost in warm, moisture-retentive soil, pressing seed onto the soil rather than burying it since light improves germination; lemon perilla is slower and less vigorous to establish than common shiso, so keep the seedbed consistently moist until seedlings are up.

directions: Lemon perilla is the least commonly cultivated of the three recognized botanical varieties of Perilla frutescens, standing apart from the familiar leaf shiso (var. crispa) and Korean kkaennip (var. japonica) by its finer, noticeably hairy stems and leaves and a bright citrus note layered over the usual perilla mint-anise base. The lemon fragrance makes it a more delicate substitute for green shiso where a lighter, brighter aroma is wanted, torn fresh over cold noodle dishes, steeped for herbal tea, or used sparingly as a fish garnish. It is less vigorous and slower to bulk up than standard shiso, so give plants a head start with consistent moisture and a bit of afternoon shade in hot climates to keep the foliage tender. Pinch flower spikes to extend leaf production, though a few plants can be left to seed for next year's crop since it self-sows readily once established.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops — Perilla frutescens
Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Perilla frutescens
Cornell Cooperative Extension Asian Vegetable Project

planting.note: Press seed onto the soil surface without covering after the last frost, since kkaennip needs light to germinate; '38N' branches heavily from the base, so give it the full recommended spacing to develop the bushy, multi-stemmed shape that supports repeated cutting.

directions: '38N' is a named Korean perilla strain maintained by Namu Farm and selected specifically for branching low from the base into a dense, bushy plant rather than growing as a single tall stalk, which means more growing points and a longer window of continuous leaf harvest than an unselected kkaennip planting. The broad leaves are green on top with a distinctive golden-lilac cast on the underside, and carry the large, thick-textured, strongly aromatic character typical of Korean perilla — used as ssam wraps for grilled meat, pickled into jangajji, and shredded into banchan. Harvest leaves in the cool of early morning for the best flavor and the longest shelf life, snipping from the outside of the plant to keep new growth coming from the base. It self-seeds enthusiastically once established, so deadhead spent flower spikes in gardens where volunteer seedlings would be unwelcome.
sources: Second Generation Seeds — Asian Vegetable Seeds
Korea Rural Development Administration (RDA) — Perilla Cultivation Guide

planting.note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost, covering seed lightly with potting mix, and transplant out once the soil has warmed; the head start is what lets this strain reliably finish seed in short-summer regions where perilla's daylength-triggered flowering otherwise runs out of season.

directions: Early Select is a regionally adapted kkaennip strain developed by growers at roughly 44°N latitude who noticed that ordinary Korean perilla, being highly sensitive to daylength, often failed to finish and dry viable seed before fall frost that far north. This selection was chosen over several seasons for plants that reliably complete their seed cycle in a shorter window, while still producing the large, strongly mint-and-basil-scented green leaves used fresh in wraps, pickled into kimchi, or pressed for their seed oil. Starting seed indoors well ahead of the last frost gives plants the extra weeks they need, and transplanting into a full-sun to partial-shade bed keeps growth vigorous through summer. Because it was bred as a dependable seed-saving strain, allow at least a few plants to flower and fully dry their seed heads at season's end to keep the line going.
sources: Adaptive Seeds — Perilla 'Early Select Kkaennip' Variety Notes
Oregon State University Extension — Specialty and Ethnic Crops
Korea Rural Development Administration (RDA) — Perilla Cultivation Guide

planting.note: Start indoors in warmth and transplant only after all frost danger has passed and nights stay reliably warm, since kemangi is even more cold-sensitive than common sweet basil; in the tropics it is grown as a short-lived perennial and cut back hard between flushes.

directions: Kemangi is the everyday table basil of Indonesia, grown less as a cooked cooking herb and more as a fresh vegetable — whole sprigs are served raw alongside cabbage, cucumber, and sambal as part of a lalapan plate, or tucked into fried fish and grilled chicken preparations to cut the richness. Its aroma sits apart from Thai basil's clove-anise punch, being lighter and more herbaceous with a gentle lime-like edge, which is exactly what makes it pleasant to eat by the sprig rather than just as a background seasoning. The thin stems and smaller leaves bruise and wilt quickly once cut, so harvest close to serving time and handle it gently. Pinch flower buds regularly to keep the plant leafy and productive through the growing season, and expect it to bolt readily in long summer daylength like other basils.
sources: University of Hawaii Cooperative Extension — Basil Types for Warm Climates
Southeast Asian Ministers of Education Organization (SEAMEO) Regional Center for Tropical Biology — Indonesian Vegetable Crops
Purdue University Center for New Crops — Ocimum basilicum
